19.0.s.en: 1. Between the way of truth and the crooked way

19.0.0.en: 1 Better is the poor that walketh in his integrity, than he that is perverse in his lips, and is a fool. 2 Also, that the soul be without knowledge, it is not good; and he that hasteth with his feet sinneth. 3 The foolishness of man perverteth his way: and his heart fretteth against the Lord.

19.0.1.en: "Better is the poor that walketh in his integrity, than he that is perverse in his lips, and is a fool" [1].

19.0.2.en: He compares a man who is materially poor yet walks in uprightness, seeking the life of perfection, with a man who boasts of the wealth and knowledge he has while he is a fool. For wisdom, or uprightness in life (godliness), or perfection, is better than the riches of the world.

19.0.3.en: Faith consists of many things, and reaches perfection in many ways. It is like a building constructed of many pieces of skillful work, rising to the summit.

19.0.4.en: * Know, my beloved, that stones are laid in the foundations of a building, and the whole structure rises upon the stones until it is complete. So our Lord Jesus Christ, the chief Stone, is the foundation of all our faith. Upon Him faith is founded. Upon Him the whole structure of faith stands until it is completed.

19.0.5.en: For the foundation is the beginning of the whole building... Its structure cannot be shaken by the waves, nor harmed by the winds, nor brought down by the storms, because the building is raised upon the rock of the true Stone.

19.0.6.en: If I have called Christ the Stone, this saying is not of my own; the prophets foretold it before me and called Him "the Stone."

19.0.7.en: St. Aphrahat * I will not be content with anything moderate remaining in you, but I long for you to rise high in everything and to be perfect in every matter.

19.0.8.en: St. Jerome * It is written: Blessed is the man who does not walk in the counsel of the wicked. Blessed is the man whom You chasten and teach out of Your law. Blessed are they who are not defiled in the way.

19.0.9.en: Blessed are those who trust in You.

19.0.10.en: Blessed is the people whose God is the Lord.

19.0.11.en: Blessed is he who does not judge.

19.0.12.en: Blessed is the man who fears the Lord (Ps 1:1; 94:12; Sir 14:1-2; Ps 112:1)...

19.0.13.en: Do you not see how the divine laws proclaim everywhere the blessedness, not of the rich, nor of the nobles, nor of those who hold glory, but of him who acquires virtue? For what is required of us is the foundation. If you plant this as a root, then not only the easy, honored, and glorious life will be your delight, but even enmities, calamities, insults, shame, and torments, all of these without exception will gladden you!

19.0.14.en: And just as the roots of trees are bitter in themselves, yet produce sweet fruits, so sound sorrow brings superabundant happiness...

19.0.15.en: And as I always say, it is not the nature of things but our own disposition that makes us sorrowful or joyful.

19.1.0.en: St. John Chrysostom "Also, that the soul be without knowledge, it is not good; and he that hasteth with his feet sinneth" [2]

19.1.1.en: He criticizes the man who is stripped of knowledge and who, in his zeal, hastens in his decisions or moves without understanding or wisdom. For it befits a man to be wise and to deliberate in his decisions, and not to move before he has thought with balance.

19.2.0.en: "The foolishness of man perverteth his way: and his heart fretteth against the Lord" [3].

19.2.1.en: Being stripped of heavenly wisdom leads a man into the crooked way, and in his self-assurance and his clinging to his own thought, his heart frets against the Lord Himself. A clear example of this is Saul of Tarsus. He was brought up at the feet of Gamaliel, a teacher of the Law, and was a Pharisee zealous for the traditions of his fathers, the honor of his people, and the keeping of the Law, perhaps reckoning himself the most righteous man in the world after his teacher; yet in ignorance he blasphemed God, persecuted the Church of Christ, and slandered the believers, as he himself later confessed.

19.2.2.en: * When they hear Christ declaring in the Gospel, "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest," at once they cast off the weight of their sins and realize what follows: "For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light" (Mt 11:28, 30).

19.2.3.en: So the way of the Lord is restful to him who keeps His commandment. But if, through some wearisome neglect, we bring sorrows and toils upon ourselves, we exert great effort following a crooked way to keep the commandments of the world, and on this way we make the yoke of Christ heavy and His burden hard, as the passage says: "The foolishness of man perverteth his way: and his heart fretteth against the Lord" (Prov 19:3). And when it is said, "The way of the Lord is not equal," He answers, "Is not my way equal? are not your ways unequal?" (Ezek 18:25).

19.2.4.en: In truth you can discern how much easier the yoke of Christ is, and how much lighter His burden, if you compare the sweet, fragrant flower of virginity and the purity of chastity with the filth of defiled, foul-smelling lust, and if you compare the quiet and stillness of the monks and their distance from the dangers and losses that occupy the minds of people in the world, with the cares of wealth and its gnawing disturbances, full of anxiety...

19.2.5.en: Father Abraham * We should admonish the wrathful in one way, and the gentle in another.

19.2.6.en: We must tell the wrathful that when they neglect to purify their souls, they rush recklessly into many errors, even ones they do not intend, for it is clear that recklessness drives the mind to where it neither wills nor desires to go.

19.2.7.en: In such a case, those who fall into recklessness do deeds whose end they do not perceive, and they will repent of them when they acknowledge having done them. And when the ungentle act under the influence of passions, they do so contrary to their nature, and they scarcely perceive the error they have committed. And when they do not resist mental disturbances, they overturn the good things they could have done in a state of clarity of mind. By sudden emotion they destroy what they have built by continuous, long-extended labor. Even the virtue of love, which is the mother of all virtues, hides itself because of anger, for it is written: "Love suffereth long, and is kind" (1 Cor 13:4). Therefore, if love is lacking, gentleness is lacking. And because of the lack of gentleness, teaching, which is the nursing of the virtues, vanishes, for Scripture says: "The discretion of a man deferreth his anger" (Prov 19:11).

19.2.8.en: For to the extent that a man lacks gentleness, he appears to chafe at teaching, and in truth he cannot acquire what is good through teaching if he has not learned in his own life how to bear the evils of others with a calm mind and quietness.

19.3.s.en: 2. The love of money corrupts life

19.3.0.en: 4 Wealth maketh many friends; but the poor is separated from his neighbour. 5 A false witness shall not be unpunished, and he that speaketh lies shall not escape. 6 Many will intreat the favour of the prince: and every man is a friend to him that giveth gifts. 7 All the brethren of the poor do hate him: how much more do his friends go far from him? He that followeth after sayings, they are his.

19.3.1.en: "Wealth maketh many friends; but the poor is separated from his neighbour" [4]

19.3.2.en: In (vv. 4-7) the wise man highlights how the love of money has corrupted life in the world, giving examples of this. The first is that people, often in partiality, seek the favor of the rich and covet their friendship, while they flee from clinging even to their poor relatives. Man has given money an estimation that exceeds the feelings of friendship, affection, and love.

19.3.3.en: "My brethren, have not the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory, with respect of persons. For if there come unto your assembly a man with a gold ring, in goodly apparel, and there come in also a poor man in vile raiment; and ye have respect to him that weareth the gay clothing, and say unto him, Sit thou here in a good place; and say to the poor, Stand thou there, or sit here under my footstool: are ye not then partial in yourselves, and are become judges of evil thoughts? Hearken, my beloved brethren, Hath not God chosen the poor of this world rich in faith, and heirs of the kingdom which he hath promised to them that love him?" (Ba 2:1-5)

19.3.4.en: * There is no great without the small, nor small without the great, but we are bound to one another for the benefit of all. Let us take the body as an example: the head cannot exist without the feet, nor the feet without the head, "nay, much more those members of the body, which seem to be more feeble, are necessary" (1 Cor 12:21-22), and useful to the whole body. Yes, all the members work in harmony and are joined to one another in perfect obedience for the well-being of the whole body.

19.3.5.en: In this way we also keep our Christian body in its perfection, each of us submitting to his fellow according to his own particular gift. The strong must care for the weak, and the weak must respect the strong. The rich supports the poor, and the poor gives thanks to God who gave him one to support him. The wise man does not show his wisdom in words but in good deeds. The humble man does not boast of his humility but leaves others to bear witness for him. The chaste man likewise does not boast, knowing that his self-control is a gift from another (God). We must love the brethren from the heart, those who were created from the same matter from which we were created.

19.3.6.en: St. Clement, bishop of Rome The rich and wise man does not squander his wealth, but gains friends with it. As the Lord of glory says: "Make to yourselves friends of the mammon of unrighteousness; that, when ye fail, they may receive you into everlasting habitations" (Lk 16:9).

19.3.7.en: For money is a gift that can be holy if it is used well, and can be evil if it is used for display, arrogance, and indulgence in pleasures and lusts.

19.3.8.en: * Wealth is not property; it is not possessions, but a loan for use. For how can you claim it as possessions when, at your death, whether you wish it or not, everything goes to others, and they in turn leave it to others again? We are all wanderers... Ownership in reality is nothing but a word; we are all owners, but of the possessions of other people... So wealth is not ours, and possessions are not property but a loan. Virtue alone is able to depart with us and accompany us in the world above.

19.3.9.en: * Is not the earth and its fullness God's? If then our possessions belong to the common Lord of all, they belong also to our fellow servants. The possessions of the Lord are common to all.

19.3.10.en: * If you grieve over some wealth, you profit nothing. If it is because of sickness, you gain nothing, but your grief only increases. I have heard many, after long experience, blaming themselves and saying: What benefit did we gain from our grief (over money or health, etc.)? I have only harmed myself.

19.4.0.en: St. John Chrysostom "A false witness shall not be unpunished, and he that speaketh lies shall not escape" [5]

19.4.1.en: As he speaks of the misuse of money, or the love of money, he points to false witness and lying, whose motive is often material gain or partiality toward the rich and those in authority, and disregard for the rights of the poor and the oppressed.

19.4.2.en: Queen Jezebel hired false witnesses against Naboth the Jezreelite in order to seize his field after killing him! She killed and inherited!

19.4.3.en: * Everyone must give great attention lest "lying" rob him, for the liar is not united with God.

19.4.4.en: The liar is a stranger to God. And Holy Scripture says that the liar is of Satan, since he is "a liar, and the father of it" (Jn 8:44).

19.4.5.en: Thus Satan was called the father of lies, but the Truth is God, for He Himself says: "I am the way, the truth, and the life" (Jn 14:6).

19.4.6.en: Do you not see, then, how we become strangers to God through lying, and with whom we are united (through it)?! Therefore, if we truly wish to be saved, we must love the truth with all our strength and all our zeal, and guard ourselves from every lie, lest it separate us from the Truth and the Life.

19.5.0.en: Father Dorotheus "Many will intreat the favour of the prince: and every man is a friend to him that giveth gifts" [6]

19.5.1.en: Just as the love of money draws many to befriend the rich, so preoccupation with personal interests draws many to befriend the nobles who hold authority and to flatter them. But the Lord Christ came to befriend sinners, the despised, and the needy (Lk 15:1). The Apostle James criticized the Church when it behaved with partiality toward the rich (Jas 2:1-6).

19.5.2.en: * Let us strip the noble women of their ornaments and the masters of their slaves, and you will notice that these will not differ in any way from slaves bought with money, neither in their manner of walking, nor in their features, nor in their speech. Rather, they resemble in everything those who are subject to them. And if they differ from them in anything, it is only that they are weaker in build and less strong than the others (the slaves), because they were brought up in a luxury that exposes them to sickness.

19.6.0.en: St. Clement of Alexandria "All the brethren of the poor do hate him: how much more do his friends go far from him? He that followeth after sayings, they are his" [7]

19.6.1.en: Not only strangers and friends withdraw from the poor man, but even relatives and brothers according to the flesh. They ignore him. Our rich Christ, the Giver of riches, became poor, that through His poverty He might enrich us (2 Cor 8:9). So we find our happiness in meeting Him through His poor brethren, and we are enriched by His love which He pours into us, so that we love everyone, especially the needy, without waiting for a reward!

19.7.s.en: 3. Wisdom and the salvation of the soul

19.7.0.en: "He that getteth wisdom loveth his own soul;

19.7.1.en: he that keepeth understanding shall find good" [8]

19.7.2.en: In our study of the Book of Wisdom we saw how the wise man links wisdom with righteousness: the man who is wise in the Lord enjoys divine righteousness, so he fears God and loves humanity. But how can he fear God unless he perceives the truth of his precious soul, the object of God's love and passion? And how can his heart open to others unless he discovers the kingdom of love that exists within him? The wise man cannot separate his care for his own depths from his care for others.

19.7.3.en: He who acquires God's wisdom does good to his inner depths, for he perceives God's care for him and His esteem of him. Thus he keeps God's commandment with understanding, and the commandment keeps him, and his depths guard him like a precious treasure.

19.7.4.en: Wisdom restores to man his true inner dignity before God as before himself, before he receives any honor from men.

19.7.5.en: He who sows wisdom by the Holy Spirit of God enjoys its fruit, by receiving countless good things from the work of the Savior.

19.8.0.en: "A false witness shall not be unpunished, and he that speaketh lies shall perish" [9]

19.8.1.en: A man bears false witness, that is, he speaks a lie, and so causes harm to the righteous, either to obtain a bribe or material gain, or to win the favor of a rich man, a friend, or a relative. But the lie will surely be exposed, and God's grace forsakes him, so he falls into troubles from which he does not escape. Finally he goes to where the devil, the father of liars, is, that is, to the darkness, and perishes eternally.

19.9.s.en: 5. The luxury of the fool and the rule of the servant

19.9.0.en: "Delight is not seemly for a fool;

19.9.1.en: much less for a servant to have rule over princes!" [10]

19.9.2.en: Two grave matters in a man's life as in society: first, that a fool should live in luxury, even if he is of noble and rich origin, squandering the resources of society without benefit to himself or others, and temporal goods only increase his folly. And second, that a man who is a slave (to his lusts, or his possessions, or temporal honor), who has not tasted the sweetness of inner freedom, should occupy a position of leadership, so that his leadership becomes the humiliation of people, without compassion, kindness, or justice!

19.10.0.en: "The discretion of a man deferreth his anger; and it is his glory to pass over a transgression" [11].

19.10.1.en: He who has learned in the school of the long-suffering God, and responded to the Holy Spirit, and so received the fruit of love, if he becomes angry, prolongs his patience and controls himself, makes excuses for others, and does all he can to win the one who wronged him; and if he reaches the point of forgiving the one who wronged him, he has attained inner glory. He has fulfilled the divine commandment: "Agree with thine adversary quickly, whiles thou art in the way with him" (Mt 5:25).

19.10.2.en: * Do not think that anger is a matter to be made light of, for the prophet says, "My eyes are troubled (withered) with anger" (Ps 6:7). And surely one whose eyes are sick cannot look upon the sun. If he tries to see it, it hurts him and does not delight him.

19.10.3.en: St. Augustine * The deadly poison of anger must be uprooted from the depths of the soul, for if the spirit of anger remains and settles in our hearts, our minds are darkened and lose their power of sight, for anger strikes with blindness and a harmful darkness that makes spiritual vision impossible. We cannot make a right judgment in any matter, and good contemplation, which develops wisdom in us, becomes impossible; indeed, we cannot abide in what is good, or receive the true spiritual light, for it is written: "Mine eye is troubled with anger" (Ps 6:7).

19.10.4.en: And people may praise us as wise, but we shall not be wise if we persist in anger, for it is written: "Anger dwelleth at rest in the bosom of the fool" (Eccl 7:9) LXX. And it exposes us to the loss of the inheritance of eternal life. It may appear to us that we understand human nature and perceive its mysteries, but if anger remains in us, what is written is fulfilled in us: "Anger destroys the wise" (Prov 15:1) LXX. And anger deprives us of perceiving the "righteousness of God," for because of anger we lose discernment, and though people may say of us that we are holy and perfect, yet it is written, "The wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God" (Jas 1:20).

19.10.5.en: St. John Cassian * I asked God to make known to me the answer to your question, and He said to me: Cleanse your heart of all the thoughts of the old man and I will answer the question of your heart, for My gifts are in the pure and are given to them, and as long as your heart is stirred by anger, hatred, and the rest of the old passions, wisdom will not enter it.

19.10.6.en: If you desire to receive My grace and My gifts, cast out the foot of the enemy and drive him away from you, and My gifts will come to you...

19.10.7.en: He who longs for My gifts, let him follow in My footsteps, for I am like the lamb in whom there is no evil...

19.10.8.en: And although I commanded you to be gentle like doves, I find that you have taken for yourselves the cruelty of the passions.

19.11.s.en: 7. Winning those in authority in the Lord

19.11.0.en: "The king's wrath is as the roaring of a lion; but his favour is as dew upon the grass" [12]

19.11.1.en: Although the believer takes pride in belonging to God and is not afraid of people or of death, yet in a spirit of humility he is committed to submitting to those in authority in the Lord, giving honor to whom honor is due, and so he finds rest and spends his days in quietness and assurance, in all godliness and dignity (see 1 Tim 2:2). Some rabbis used to pray: "O Lord, bless the emperor, and keep him far from us."

19.11.2.en: If this is the believer's attitude toward a king or ruler, even if he is an unbeliever, what should his attitude be toward the King of kings and Lord of lords? He is the Lion who came out of the tribe of Judah; He came for the salvation of humanity, not for its judgment. But He will come on the Day of Judgment, and the souls of the true believers will rejoice, while the wicked will count it the day of His great wrath: who is able to stand before Him?

19.11.3.en: Tertullian says: [Therefore, concerning the honors due to kings and emperors, we have sufficient text that it befits us to be in complete obedience, according to the commandment of the Apostle, "to be subject to principalities and powers" (Titus 3:1); but the limit of obedience in this is that we keep ourselves apart from the worship of idols. We have in this also the example of the three youths, who, while obeying King Nebuchadnezzar, disdained to offer honor to his image and did not accept to worship it... So also Daniel was subject to Darius in all things, steadfast in his duty so long as it was far from the foundation of his faith (Dan 6).]

19.12.0.en: A foolish son is the calamity of his father: and the contentions of a wife are a continual dropping. 14 House and riches are the inheritance of fathers: and a prudent wife is from the Lord.

19.12.1.en: "A foolish son is the calamity of his father: and the contentions of a wife are a continual dropping" [13]

19.12.2.en: How wretched is the house that includes a foolish son and a contentious wife. Often the two agree together; for where there are quarrels in the family, the children become loose, and try to play a dangerous role between the parents, to show each of them that they are on his side, and so they win affection and benefit by obtaining concessions, and the sense of obligation and responsibility is removed from the children.

19.12.3.en: * If the Apostle commands us to care for others more than for ourselves, and if we are counted at fault when we neglect what is for their benefit, shall we not be much more at fault if this concerns those who are close to us?

19.12.4.en: The Lord will say to us: "Was it not I who gave these children a place in your family? Was it not I who entrusted them to your care, and made you masters, guardians, and judges over them? I gave you complete authority over them. I handed them wholly into your hands for their upbringing.

19.12.5.en: You will tell me that they did not want to bow their necks to the yoke, and that they cast it off. But this could have been avoided from the very beginning. It was fitting for you to bow their little souls under the yoke of obligation, to accustom them to it, to teach them this, and to bandage the wound at the beginning of its opening.

19.12.6.en: It was fitting for you to pull up the tares when they began to appear around the plants, and it was not fitting for you to wait until their roots deepened, so that it became impossible to control and tame the passions by strengthening them (the children) gradually during their formation and growth.

19.12.7.en: St. John Chrysostom Calm, constructive dialogue is beneficial for the family, in which each party respects the others and does not cling to his own opinion, so that the children learn the spirit of holy dialogue. But quarrels, strife, anger, and the withdrawal of one from another cause the home to lose the presence of the Lord Christ in their midst, and corrupt the spirit of godliness in all, fathers and children, and instill in the new generation the spirit of rebellion and clinging to one's own opinion.

19.12.8.en: He likens the contentious wife to drops of water that fall continually without stopping. The husband, like the children, feels that they are in a house from whose roof drops of water fall without ceasing, so that they do not know how to work or rest or sleep, finding no dry place in the house to take refuge in.

19.12.9.en: From the words of St. Gregory of Nazianzus in praise of his parents:

19.12.10.en: [Behold, the good shepherd is the fruit of the prayers of his wife and her guidance, and he learned from her his ideal pastoral life. With power he fled from the worship of idols, and afterward the demons fled from him.. They became equal in prudence and splendor, zealous, supporting one another, flying above all...

19.12.11.en: They had two bodies, but it was as though the two bodies had been turned into one spirit, even before their dissolution... They possessed everything and lacked nothing. They rejected wealth, and so became rich in honor...

19.12.12.en: I say only one word about them: that in right and justice each of them was appointed for his own kind. He was appointed an ornament for men, and she an ornament for women, not only an ornament, but also an example of the virtuous life.]

19.13.0.en: "House and riches are the inheritance of fathers: and a prudent wife is from the Lord" [14]

19.13.1.en: A man inherits a house, lands, or money from his parents, but the wise wife is a divine gift, which the Lord gives to him who truly lives in the spirit of godliness, and has a sound view of the meaning of marriage, and asks God to guide him and choose for him. When the will is submitted to the Lord, the Lord provides the wife or the husband according to what He sees for the salvation of the whole house.

19.13.2.en: God has holy sons and daughters, dear to Him, whom He wishes to give to the one who asks in submission to His will, and He gives him or her what suits the person.

19.13.3.en: How beautiful it is for a man to offer God a daily sacrifice of thanksgiving for the gift of the life partner whom he received from God's hand!

19.13.4.en: * When the Apostle spoke of marriage and virginity he said: "But every man hath his proper gift of God, one after this manner, and another after that" (1 Cor 7:7). He says that marriage is a gift. For it is written: "A wife is given to a man from the Lord" (Prov 19:14), but this gift is not a spiritual gift in a strict sense, for there are many things that can be called gifts from God, such as wealth, bodily strength, physical beauty, and temporal authority. These gifts too are from God, and as Daniel says: "He removeth kings, and setteth up kings" (Dan 2:21).

19.14.0.en: "Slothfulness casteth into a deep sleep; and an idle soul shall suffer hunger" [15]

19.14.1.en: Many do not realize the value of work and commitment, nor the value of time, and that negligence in work, wasting time, and lack of commitment are all things that corrupt a man's spiritual, social, psychological, and bodily health, and make him lose even what he has received, and he gives account for all this!

19.14.2.en: The Apostle says: "Redeeming the time, because the days are evil" (Eph 5:16); "Walk in wisdom toward them that are without, redeeming the time" (Col 4:6).

19.14.3.en: * What we often gain through zeal, laziness destroys, and what hesitation loses, diligence restores.

19.15.0.en: 16 He that keepeth the commandment keepeth his own soul; but he that despiseth his ways shall die. 17 He that hath pity upon the poor lendeth unto the Lord; and that which he hath given will he pay him again.

19.15.1.en: "He that keepeth the commandment keepeth his own soul; but he that despiseth his ways shall die" [16]

19.15.2.en: He who keeps the divine commandment, the commandment keeps him eternally. In obedience to the commandment is the delight of love for God, a tasting of the blessing of obedience, and enjoyment of victory over death in Christ, the Giver of victory. But he who treats the commandment lightly treats God Himself lightly, and casts himself into the pit of eternal death.

19.15.3.en: * We ought to look to God's commandments when they are read, or when memory recalls them, as one who looks in a mirror, as the Apostle James says. Such a man wishes to look at God's commandments as in a mirror and is not confused, for he chooses not only to be a hearer of the commandments but also a doer of them. Therefore he desires that his ways be directed toward keeping God's statutes. How are they directed except by God's grace? Otherwise he finds in God's law not a source of joy but a source of confusion, if he chooses to look at the commandments and not do them.

19.15.4.en: St. Augustine * He who keeps one commandment and leaves others has betrayed all the commandments, for he insults God, who commanded them and bound them to one another. For He who said, Do not commit adultery, said also, Do not steal; if you steal you become a debtor to the whole law; but he who is careful of all the commandments will not be ashamed on the dreadful day of judgment.

19.16.0.en: Anthimus, bishop of Jerusalem "He that hath pity upon the poor lendeth unto the Lord; and that which he hath given will he pay him again" [17].

19.16.1.en: He links the keeping of the commandment with mercy, especially toward the poor. For the Creator of the poor counts every kindness shown to the poor as offered to Himself personally, and considers it a loan that He repays doubled. David the psalmist says: "I have been young, and now am old; yet have I not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his seed begging bread. He is ever merciful, and lendeth; and his seed is blessed" (Ps 37:25-26).

19.16.2.en: * Hold fast, then, to asking Him for the debt, for it is not fitting that we leave Him and ask repayment from another besides Him, for He sees in what you do an error, as though He says to you: Why do you do this, and with what ingratitude do you accuse Me? Do you claim that I am poor, so that you intend to take the debt from others? Do you lend to (the one God) and then ask another to repay this loan? For though it is man who received the loan, it is God who commanded you to give to him, and His will is that He Himself be the debtor in the fullest sense of the word; and in truth the Lord gives you manifold opportunities to recover the debt from Him at all times and in all places. So do not let this opportune moment slip from you so easily, nor squander this abundant generosity by asking for the debt from those who have nothing. For what purpose do you show mercy to the poor? What? Was it not I who said to you, Give? Did you not hear that from Me, that you should recover your gifts from Me? Did I not say, "He that hath pity upon the poor lendeth unto the Lord" (Prov 19:17)? And you have lent to God, so put this debt on His account, even if He does not repay you the whole debt now. Well, He does that for your good also. What a debtor! Not like many who simply wish to pay back what they borrowed; rather the Lord arranges everything, to invest it securely, because it is a loan given to the Lord. Therefore, as you see, He repays some of it here and defers the debt for the rest.

19.17.0.en: 18 Chasten thy son, for there is hope in him; but let not thy soul be set upon his death. 19 A man of great wrath shall suffer punishment: for if thou deliver him, yet thou must do it again.

19.17.1.en: "Chasten thy son, for there is hope in him; but let not thy soul be set upon his death" [18]

19.17.2.en: In a spirit of hope a man disciplines his son with firmness mingled with tenderness and love. But violent, extreme punishments bear the guilt of murder, and also provoke the children and drive them to stubbornness, so that discipline is not for reform but for destruction.

19.17.3.en: In discipline a constructive dialogue must be entered into, so that the son understands what is behind the discipline, and the father understands what is behind his son's conduct, so that he does not discipline in haste and emotion. Loose liberty and violent severity are both ruinous and destructive to children as to the family.

19.17.4.en: King Saul, in his anger, instead of open dialogue with his son Jonathan, aimed the spear at him to smite him (1 Sam 20:33), and so the son lost his confidence in his father and withdrew from him in heart.

19.17.5.en: * God bears all the weaknesses of men, but He will not allow the perpetual murmurer to be left without discipline.

19.18.0.en: St. Mar Isaac the Syrian "A man of great wrath shall suffer punishment: for if thou deliver him, yet thou must do it again" [19]

19.18.1.en: Some link this proverb with the one before it, and interpret it thus: if the son is of great wrath, he must be disciplined or punished with wisdom and deliberation until he ceases from anger; if he is not disciplined he will repeat this emotion and fall under a bitter punishment, that is, he will punish himself by himself. It is as though whoever is not disciplined by his parents will discipline himself, or as it is said: "He whom his parents do not discipline, time disciplines."

19.19.0.en: 20 Hear counsel, and receive instruction, that thou mayest be wise in thy latter end. 21 There are many devices in a man's heart; nevertheless the counsel of the Lord, that shall stand.

19.19.1.en: "Hear counsel, and receive instruction, that thou mayest be wise in thy latter end" [20]

19.19.2.en: Some see this proverb as the key to the whole book: the call to accept counsel so that the believer may become wise. Fools despise counsel, but the wise man accepts counsel with joy, and thinks seriously about rebuke or reproof, and even about the discipline that comes upon him, because he loves to learn and to benefit from the experience of others.

19.20.0.en: "There are many devices in a man's heart; nevertheless the counsel of the Lord, that shall stand" [21]

19.20.1.en: Often a man wavers in his thoughts; what he accepts now he may reject after a few minutes, or the reverse. He may listen to many counselors and be seized by a kind of confusion and disturbance. But when he takes refuge in God, who alone knows the truth and who loves His creation, He gives true, successful, and steadfast counsel.

19.21.0.en: "The adornment of a man is his kindness: and a poor man is better than a liar" [22].

19.21.1.en: The adornment of the spirit is well known: it is love, tenderness, and mercy with giving. The spirit is adorned by removing all selfishness, so as to expand and contain others within it. Along with this practical love the spirit must be truthful with itself; if a man is unable to give a certain gift, let him be frank and excuse himself for his poverty or inability, and not promise others while he knows he is unable to carry it out.

19.21.2.en: With complete frankness Peter declared to the lame man his inability to give material gifts, but he offered him something greater, for he said to him: "Silver and gold have I none; but such as I have give I thee: In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth rise up and walk" (Acts 3:6).

19.22.0.en: "The fear of the Lord tendeth to life:

19.22.1.en: and he shall abide satisfied; he shall not be visited with evil" [23]

19.22.2.en: He who fears the Lord and reveres Him takes refuge in Him and shelters in Him as his refuge and fortress. He lives in safety, lacking nothing. He feels that all things work together for good. He ever sings the song of victory, saying with the Apostle Paul: "In all these things we are more than conquerors through him that loved us. For I am persuaded, that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord" (Rom 8:27-29). Thus he who fears the Lord rejoices, for his soul is watered from the springs of God's love, and is satisfied from the heavenly table.

19.22.3.en: * The great good is not to possess money, but to acquire the fear of the Lord and all the means of godliness.

19.22.4.en: St. John Chrysostom * If anyone wishes to obtain the love of God, let the fear of the Lord be in him, for fear begets weeping, and weeping begets strength. And when all these are fulfilled in the soul, the soul begins to bear fruit in everything. And when God sees these good fruits in the soul, He smells them as the fragrance of sweet incense, and rejoices in it, He and His angels, and satisfies it with joy, and keeps it in all its ways until it reaches its place of rest without any harm coming to it.

19.22.5.en: When Satan sees the great heavenly Guardian surrounding the soul, he is afraid to approach it or attack it because of this great power.

19.22.6.en: Therefore acquire this power so that the demons tremble before you, and your works become easy, and you delight in the divine work, for the sweetness of God's love is sweeter than honey.

19.22.7.en: Truly many monks and virgins in the communities have not tasted this divine sweetness and have not acquired the divine power, supposing that they have received it, despite their lack of striving. But he who strives for it will surely receive it through the divine mercies, for God is no respecter of persons.

19.22.8.en: So whoever wishes to have God's light and power must despise the honors of this world and its defilement, hate all the things of the world and the pleasure of the flesh, and purify his heart of all evil thoughts. And he offers God fasts and tears night and day without relenting as pure prayers; then God pours that power upon him.

19.22.9.en: Strive to obtain this power, that you may do all your works with ease and facility, and have great boldness before God, and He will give you all that you ask.

19.23.0.en: "A slothful man hideth his hand in the dish, and will not so much as bring it to his mouth again" [24]

19.23.1.en: The wise man portrays the lazy man with a sumptuous table set before him, full of foods; he stretches out his hand and puts it in the dish, but from his great laziness and desire for sleep and drowsiness, he finds it hard to lift his hand to put the food in his mouth. He prefers to suffer hunger in his slackness rather than stretch out his hand with food to eat and be satisfied. So many do, for God sets before them a delicious table in Holy Scripture, the food of the soul, but in slackness and laziness they do not benefit from the opportunity offered them to eat and be satisfied.

19.24.0.en: "Smite a scorner, and the fool will become shrewd; and reprove one that hath understanding, and he will understand knowledge" [25]

19.24.1.en: If the scorner is left to practice his contempt for the commandment or for others without rebuke or discipline, he finds justification for his conduct, unconcerned about the consequences of his evils. But as for firmness with the scorner, even if the person himself does not benefit from it, others will benefit, for they fear lest punishments come upon them. And the man of understanding, when he is rebuked for a mistake he committed, benefits from the rebuke, for he always wants to learn and to grow in every good work.

19.25.0.en: 26 He that wasteth his father, and chaseth away his mother, is a son that causeth shame, and bringeth reproach. 27 Cease, my son, to hear the instruction that causeth to err from the words of knowledge.

19.25.1.en: "He that wasteth his father, and chaseth away his mother, is a son that causeth shame, and bringeth reproach" [26]

19.25.2.en: The rebellious son ruins his father, squandering his wealth and possessions to fulfill his pleasures and lusts. In his stubbornness he loses all tenderness, even toward his mother, and drives her away, thus staining the family with shame and disgrace. The rebel thinks that by this shameful conduct toward his parents he is exercising his right to freedom and breaking all restraints, and he does not know that he is practicing recklessness and laxity, and his life ends in scandal and destruction.

19.25.3.en: If rebellion against a ruler or king drives its perpetrator to being killed or executed, what then will be the punishment of the tyrant who rebels against God and His commandment?

19.25.4.en: St. Augustine says that by rebellion some of the heavenly beings lost their position and descended to eternal destruction, and no longer had the right of fellowship with the angels. Whereas (by obedience) man receives a promise that after the resurrection he will be equal to the angels.

19.26.0.en: "Cease, my son, to hear the instruction that causeth to err from the words of knowledge" [27]

19.26.1.en: The wise man offers his advice or commandment to the rebellious son, who embraces the principles and philosophies of license and rebellion, counting error away from the truth and indifference to the spiritual life as a call to practice freedom. The wise man asks him to carry the spirit of discernment, to walk in the light and reject the darkness. Let him stop his ears against misleading teachings, in order to listen and submit to the divine truth.

19.27.0.en: "A base witness scorneth the truth: and the mouth of the wicked devoureth iniquity" [28].

19.27.1.en: When the wicked man bears false witness against his neighbor, he drives himself into a chain of evils and the practice of injustice and violence, and counts his mouth, which swore falsely and testified lies, a workshop of iniquity.

19.28.0.en: "Punishment is prepared for scorners, and stripes for the back of fools." [29]

19.28.1.en: The scorners who treat the divine holy things lightly cast themselves into grave punishment, and are beaten as ignorant and foolish men.

19.28.2.en: The day of the Lord is surely coming, and judgment will truly fall on the wicked; the pleasures of sins are temporary, but their punishment is eternal!

19.28.3.en: St. John Chrysostom depicts for us the great day of the Lord on which the judgment takes place and the wicked are tried, saying:

19.28.4.en: * All things will be astonishing in the extreme and filled with terror and trembling. Even the angels themselves will be seized by fear, not only the angels but also the archangels, thrones, dominions, principalities, and powers. We read: "And the powers of the heavens shall be shaken" (Mt 24:29). For fellow servants will be asked to give an account of their lives on earth. If a single city is judged before the rulers of this world, all people tremble, even those who are out of danger; how much more if the whole world is summoned before such a Judge, who needs no witnesses nor proofs, but without all this brings up deeds and words in a form seen by those who commit sins and those who are ignorant of them, is it not natural that all the powers be astonished and tremble?

19.28.6.en: Grant me to walk in the way of truth!

19.28.7.en: * Grant me to be united with You, O divine Truth, that I may walk in the truth, and not turn to the right hand or to the left.

19.28.8.en: * I live by You in perfect freedom, so that no wealth, whatever its value, enslaves me.

19.28.9.en: I see You as my treasure and my riches.

19.28.10.en: Nothing occupies me except meeting You in Your glories.

19.28.11.en: Where my soul with my body shall enjoy eternal glories.

19.28.12.en: * I possess You, O Truth, so that lying finds no dwelling in me.

19.28.13.en: And ignorance does not creep into my depths.

19.28.14.en: And anger does not dominate my feelings.

19.28.15.en: * I love You and am occupied with You; I give honor to whom honor is due, and I honor every person, whatever his age or position.

19.28.16.en: * You are manifested in my depths, and make of me a temple for You.

19.28.17.en: And You declare Your presence in my family, so that it becomes a rejoicing heavenly church, whose canon is love, humility, and continual giving.

19.28.18.en: * Your Spirit kindles my heart with sacrificial love.

19.28.19.en: I work and give without ceasing.

19.28.20.en: I know neither deceit nor malice.

19.28.21.en: * I fear You as a son subject in love to his father.

19.28.22.en: I revere You lest I wound Your feelings.

19.28.23.en: I accept every discipline from Your hands, trusting in Your wisdom and care!
